public.title: A city remembers in public
public.story: These photographs let a stretch of pavement function as a record of attention: someone stopped, looked, and kept looking. Years later, the city’s documented STAMP programme gives another point of comparison for art in everyday public space.
public.fact: The official STAMP page reports over 200,000 sq ft along major streets and four flyover underpasses. This is a later historical project record, not a 2026 inventory.
public.question: When a wall is repainted, who keeps the memory of what people once walked past?

sources.title: Bhubaneswar Smart City Limited — I Am Bhubaneswar

public.scope: The later STAMP programme is not evidence of who painted or commissioned these 2009 works.

narrative.title: Stories that travel between surfaces
narrative.story: Raghurajpur, known for Pattachitra, offers a useful connection: Odisha Tourism describes cloth painting, palm-leaf engraving, papier-mâché masks and painted toys within its craft practice. A story can take on a new surface while remaining recognisable to its audience.
narrative.fact: Cloth, dried palm leaf and papier-mâché are three different materials documented in Raghurajpur’s craft repertoire.
narrative.question: What changes when an image made to be held or kept indoors becomes part of a stranger’s daily walk?
narrative.scope: This is regional craft context. The mural’s maker, workshop and precise stylistic lineage have not been established.

saora.title: A comparison with Saora painting
saora.story: The geometric figures and shared fields of people, animals and plants invite comparison with Saora painting. The Odisha State Tribal Museum describes idital as ceremonial paintings associated with deities, and also records work made on paper and canvas for sale.
saora.fact: The museum documents both ceremonial use and adaptations for sale; the setting of an image is part of its meaning.
saora.question: When a sacred visual language enters a public street, what context should travel with it?
saora.scope: A visual comparison, not an attribution: resemblance alone cannot identify a Saora artist, a ritual purpose, or a specific idital in these photographs.

jhoti.title: The threshold and the street
jhoti.story: Odisha’s jhoti/chita tradition connects drawing to household ritual. The state’s cultural account describes white rice paste, or pithau, used on walls and floors, including during the worship of Lakshmi in Margasira. These white ornaments invite a comparison with that intimacy of hand and surface.
jhoti.fact: Rice paste is a documented traditional material for jhoti/chita; the material used on these roadside walls is unknown.
jhoti.question: How does a motif’s meaning change when it moves from a household threshold to a public boundary?

sources.title: Government of Odisha — Jhoti, Chita, Muruja

jhoti.scope: The relationship is interpretive. These photographs do not establish ritual use or prove that the murals were made with rice paste.

maritime.title: A boat carries a memory
maritime.story: The painted boats offer a way into Odisha’s maritime memory. Bali Jatra in Cuttack commemorates the voyages of Odia traders, known as Sadhabas, and their connections with Southeast Asia. The festival begins on Kartika Purnima.
maritime.fact: Cuttack, the Mahanadi riverbank and Kartika Purnima are the place, landscape and calendar reference recorded by the Ministry of Tourism.
maritime.question: What does a community choose to remember about a voyage: the cargo, the departure, or the people who waited?

sources.title: Ministry of Tourism / Incredible India — Bali Jatra

maritime.scope: The festival supplies cultural context; it does not establish that a particular painted boat depicts a Sadhaba voyage.

palm.title: A leaf becomes a page
palm.story: The words “Our Palm Leaf Work” name the craft in the photograph itself. Odisha Tourism documents engraving on dried palm leaves among the practices of Raghurajpur. The seated maker brings the labour of storytelling into view.
palm.fact: The archive’s panel explicitly labels the craft; its exact narrative scenes and artisan identity remain unidentified.
palm.question: When we admire an illustrated story, how often do we notice the hand that prepared its page?
palm.scope: Raghurajpur is a documented craft connection, not an established origin for this mural.

pipili.title: Colour stitched into public life
pipili.story: The labelled appliqué panel opens a connection to Pipili. Odisha Tourism records the use of Pipili appliqué on the chariots of Jagannath and his siblings during Ratha Yatra, as well as in domestic objects such as hangings, umbrellas and bags.
pipili.fact: The same craft serves a ceremonial chariot and everyday objects, linking ritual patronage with daily use.
pipili.question: How much of a festival’s splendour belongs to the makers whose names the crowd may never hear?
pipili.scope: The photograph depicts the craft in paint; it is not itself a piece of stitched appliqué.

dhokra.title: The shape left by wax
dhokra.story: The panel labelled “Our Dhokra Work” points to a metal-casting practice. The Development Commissioner (Handicrafts) describes Dhokra as a lost-wax process found in Odisha and other eastern and central Indian states.
dhokra.fact: Lost-wax casting is the documented making process; a painted surface cannot establish the alloy of the objects depicted.
dhokra.question: What would we value differently if the making process were as visible as the finished object?

konark.title: Time, stone and a moving body
konark.story: The temple, wheel and dancer invite a connection to Konark. UNESCO describes the 13th-century Sun Temple as Surya’s chariot and records musicians and dancers among its sculptural imagery. This mural brings architecture and the performing body into one roadside encounter.
konark.fact: Konark has 24 carved wheels and was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1984.
konark.question: A monument can endure for centuries. What keeps the movement and knowledge represented on it alive?

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre — Sun Temple, Konârak

konark.scope: The historical facts concern Konark, not the age of this mural. The caption does not identify the dancer, choreographic pose or painter.

temple.title: A skyline held in memory
temple.story: Temple images on a city wall invite recognition from people who may know the buildings through worship, travel or family stories. As a regional reference, Odisha Tourism dates Bhubaneswar’s Lingaraj Temple to the 11th century.
temple.fact: The 11th-century date belongs to Lingaraj Temple. It must not be transferred to unidentified temple images or to these wall paintings.
temple.question: Which part of a temple stays with a person longest: its silhouette, a ceremony, a sound, or a memory of visiting?
temple.scope: This is background for Odisha’s architectural heritage, not identification of every depicted building.

craft.title: The everyday object deserves a portrait
craft.story: Odisha Tourism’s craft overview includes woodwork, terracotta, brass and bell metal, horn work, stone carving and other practices. These painted objects invite us to consider the design knowledge held in things used, played with or handled every day.
craft.fact: The pictured materials are representations in paint. A photograph of the wall cannot verify the material or workshop of the depicted object.
craft.question: Which ordinary object in your own home would deserve a place in a museum of lived experience?

performance.title: The body carries the story
performance.story: CCRT identifies Odissi as a classical dance form originating in Odisha. The dancers and musicians in this archive offer a broader invitation to think about knowledge carried through movement, rehearsal and performance.
performance.fact: The archive includes different kinds of performing figures; no single dance form has been assigned to all of them.
performance.question: What can a painted pose preserve, and what can only be learned from a living performer?

sources.title: Centre for Cultural Resources and Training — Audio-visual catalogue

performance.scope: Odissi is a cultural reference here, not a confirmed identification of every dancer, musician or mask.

contemporary.title: The archive also asks new questions
contemporary.story: The later-numbered paintings introduce globes, trees, faces, written messages and unsettled forms. Placing them beside the craft and temple imagery allows Odisha’s visual culture to include experiments and questions as well as inherited motifs.
contemporary.fact: This archive contains 28 retained contemporary-painting photographs and three alternate views, all recording 18 February 2009 in the camera metadata.
contemporary.question: Which image makes you pause because you recognise it, and which because you cannot yet explain it?
contemporary.scope: This is an editorial reading of the photographs, not a statement of the artists’ intentions. Their exhibition context and exact locations are unverified.

sculpture.title: A surface asks to be read
sculpture.story: The reliefs and garden sculptures broaden the walk from paint to volume, texture and shadow. Their presence in the same camera-day sequence preserves another way art was encountered in public space.
sculpture.fact: Nine sculpture and relief photographs are retained in the main art collection; no installation dates or sculptor identities are established.
sculpture.question: What makes us call one object heritage and another decoration, before we know either one’s history?
sculpture.scope: No photographed relief or garden sculpture is being dated as ancient or identified as an original temple carving.

nature.title: Who shares the picture?
nature.story: Across the archive, animals, birds, trees and water occupy as much imaginative space as people. In the street photographs, living leaves and shadows sometimes enter the frame too. The relationship between painted nature and the surrounding city becomes part of the viewing experience.
nature.fact: The images document painted subjects and their photographed surroundings, not a wildlife survey or an identified ecological site.
nature.question: If the city were designed with the same attention to birds, trees and animals as these pictures, what might change?

_meta.basis: Sources provide cultural background; file counts and dates are derived from this archive. Poetic captions and discussion questions are editorial interpretations.
